summary: State e12fdb0f056767c5 (source level) is 2.197x faster than amdclang (240 pairs, CI 2.192..2.202; 0.0920 ms vs 0.2021 ms), static check and full battery (49/49) pass. It launches 4 waves per query row (block 256): wave w takes key tiles w, w+4, ... with no barriers inside the tile loop (each wave is its own lockstep unit with its own LDS scratch row), hoists q (the compiler puts it in SGPRs with s_load_dwordx16), loads each key row as 16 dwordx4 loads in flight, replaces the two LDS tree reductions (7 barriers each) by one LDS write + 64 LDS reads reduced in registers in the same tree order, issues the V loads 16 at a time, uses a bare v_exp_f32 (exp2 builtin), and merges the 4 partial (m, l, o) triples through LDS after a single barrier. Results meet the manifest tolerance, not bit-identity (exp2 instead of expf, merged partial softmaxes). Headroom case: the reference headroom is 9.9 under the one-touch model, so 1.5x was possible in principle and was reached; but the model undercounts: K and V are re-read by every query row (about 1.07 GB of cache traffic at N=2048), and the remaining time looks bound by that traffic and wave count, where three further ideas plateaued.

tried.what: one wave per row, no barriers, q hoisted, 16 x4 K loads in flight, LDS write + 64 reads per reduction, all 64 V loads in flight with p kept in a 64-entry array (compiler spilled it: 320 B scratch, 14 VGPR spills)

GEMM-style: lane = query row, K/V rows uniform across the wave, 8 waves per workgroup split the key range, 135 KB LDS merge (compiler used per-lane global loads at a uniform address, not scalar loads; 91 VGPR spills, 128-VGPR cap)
first design without scratch: p re-read from LDS in chunks of 16 alongside 16 V loads in flight, exp2 builtin; 110 VGPRs, 0 spills
4 waves per row (block 256), wave w takes tiles w mod 4, partials merged via LDS after one barrier
on top of W=4: branch-free partial tile (V row index clamped, p = 0) instead of the serial tail loop
on top of W=4: low-VGPR variant (84 instead of 120 VGPRs: K in two halves, reductions in chunks of 16) for higher occupancy

friction: No machine-IR work was done: the budget went into source restructuring, and the passes (coarsen, unroll_loads) and DPP reductions were not tried on the winning state. A DPP reduction would remove the LDS write + 64 reads per reduction, but writing it by hand in a 500-instruction listing did not fit in the time.

bench's traffic/headroom model assumes each tensor element is touched once. For this kernel K and V are re-read by every query row (about N^2/2 * 512 B = 1.07 GB at N=2048 against 2.1 MB modelled), so headroom 9.9 and tb_per_s 0.01 are misleading; a per-kernel traffic expression in the manifest, or a count derived from executed loads, would have pointed at the right bound from the start.

Scratch use is only visible after check (resources.scratch_bytes, vgpr_spills); features() of state 687d7b30a308f5aa shows scratch_store/scratch_load in mnemonics but no warning. A static_check or features warning 'this state spills to scratch' would have saved two timed candidates (0.63x and 0.13x).
amdclang caps this kernel at 128 VGPRs and spills beyond it (states 687d7b30a308f5aa, 18a2c0b587d721df) although the ISA allows 256; I found no way to raise the cap from source().

In state 18a2c0b587d721df amdclang loaded a wave-uniform, loop-variant row (K[j], V[j]) with per-lane global_load_dwordx4 instead of s_load_dwordx16, although it used s_load_dwordx16 for the loop-invariant q row; there is no source-level way to ask for a scalar load, so the 'lane = query, shared K/V row' design could not be expressed without hand-written IR.
features() reports waves_per_simd 0 with limiter lds for state 18a2c0b587d721df (135168 B LDS, 8 waves per workgroup), which still ran; the number looks wrong.

No per-wave or per-phase profile: I could not tell latency, instruction throughput, dispatch of 8192 waves and cache traffic apart except by building variants. static_check also warns of an undefined read of v76 in 687d7b30a308f5aa (.LBB0_2[49]) that I did not investigate; the state passed the battery.
lessons: Scratch (stack) memory is very expensive on this device: the same design measured 0.63x with 320 B of scratch and 14 VGPR spills (687d7b30a308f5aa) and 1.76x with none (48ff2bfa34b53cf6); a state with 91 spills ran at 0.13x. Check resources.scratch_bytes after every source() and restructure (smaller in-flight chunks, re-read from LDS instead of keeping a 64-entry array) until it is 0. That scratch is the cause is inferred from this pair, which also differ in chunking and exp; it was not isolated.
amdclang keeps at most 128 VGPRs for these kernels and spills beyond; arrays of 64 per-lane values indexed by a variable go to scratch.

A workgroup of exactly one wave (block 64) needs no barriers around LDS: replacing a barrier tree reduction (7 barriers) by one LDS write and 64 LDS reads (ds_read_b128) reduced in registers in the same tree order is legal as long as the reads may alias the write (so the compiler cannot reorder them), and was part of a 1.76x win.

A wave-uniform, loop-invariant row is loaded by amdclang with s_load_dwordx16 into SGPRs and used directly as fmac operands (q row: 4 scalar loads instead of 64 per-lane loads per tile). A uniform but loop-variant row is not: it stays a per-lane global load.

Splitting a long per-row loop over several waves of one workgroup with a single final LDS merge paid 1.76x -> 2.20x at 4 waves (causal attention, longest row 32 tiles); 8 waves measured 2.07x, so the gain saturates once the wave count (8192 here) reaches the device's wave slots.
Past that point, higher occupancy (120 -> 84 VGPRs, 2.16x vs 2.20x) and removing a serial tail loop (2.18x vs 2.20x) each brought nothing.
The headroom figure is not reliable for kernels that re-read inputs (attention, GEMM-like): compute the real traffic by hand before choosing a lever.

session.final:
The kernel is now 2.20x faster than amdclang's build (0.0920 ms against 0.2021 ms, 240 pairs, CI 2.192 to 2.202), above the 1.5x target. The state to ship is `e12fdb0f056767c5`; it passes the static check and the full battery (49/49), and the report is filed.

What the winning state does differently, all at the source level:
- **Four waves per query row** (block 256): each wave takes every fourth key tile, and the four partial results are merged through LDS after a single barrier.
- **No barriers inside the tile loop**: the two barrier-tree reductions are replaced by one LDS write and 64 LDS reads, reduced in registers.
- **Loads in flight**: the query row is loaded once, each key row as 16 wide loads, and the V loads 16 at a time.
- **Cheaper exp**: the exp2 builtin instead of `expf`.

Results meet the manifest tolerance but are not bit-identical to the baseline.

On the headroom question: the reference headroom is 9.9, so 1.5x was possible in principle. That figure is misleading here, though, because every query row re-reads K and V — about 1.07 GB of cache traffic at N=2048 against the 2.1 MB the model assumes.

| Idea | State | Speedup |
|---|---|---|
| One wave per row, no barriers, but spilling to scratch | `687d7b30a308f5aa` | 0.63 (loss) |
| Lane = query row, K/V rows shared across the wave | `18a2c0b587d721df` | 0.13 (loss) |
| One wave per row with no scratch | `48ff2bfa34b53cf6` | 1.76 |
| Four waves per row | `e12fdb0f056767c5` | 2.20 |
| Four waves, branch-free partial tile | `f88083ab136163b5` | 2.18 |
| Four waves, fewer registers for occupancy | `23f11eec31b453fd` | 2.16 |
| Eight waves per row | `8f6db42e52456eb4` | 2.07 |

The first loss and the first win are the same design; the win has no scratch spills (the loss had 14), which is the likely cause but was not isolated. I stopped after the last three variants each failed to beat the four-wave state.
